Consider the set of matrices $\big\{A, B \big\},$ where 
$$
A= {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}1 & 0 \\ - 2 & 4\end{array} \right]}, 
	\qquad
	B= {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}3 & 5 \\ 2 & - 6\end{array} \right]}.
$$
If the set is linearly dependent, find the value of $\dfrac{x_1}{x_2}$ from a non-zero solution of $x_1A+x_2B=O,$ where $O$ is the $2 \times 2$ zero-matrix.

If the set is linearly dependent, then there exist $x_1,x_2,x_3$ not all zero such that 

$$
x_1p_1(t)+x_2p_2(t)+x_3p_3(t)=0.
$$

Otherwise, if $x_1 = x_2 = x_3 = 0,$ the set is linearly independent.

Substituting the given expressions for $p_1(t),p_2(t),$ and $p_3(t)$ into the above equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(1+t)+{x}_{2}(-2t-4)+{x}_{3}(-2t-3) & =0 \\ ({x}_{1}-4{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3})+({x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3})t & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The final equation is true for every $t$ if and only if 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3} &=0 \\ {x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3} &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Now, we consider the corresponding augmented matrix and reduce it to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -4 & -3 & 0 \\ 1 & -2 & -2 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -4 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The pivot columns are the $1$st and $2$nd. Hence, $x_3$ is a free variable. The system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3} &=0 \\ 2{x}_{2}+{x}_{3} &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the second equation, we get $x_2=-\dfrac 12x_3.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
x_1-4\left(-\dfrac 12x_3\right)-3x_3=0 \qquad\Longrightarrow \qquad x_1=x_3.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is
$$
{\left[ \begin{array}{c}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{array} \right]}
	=
	{\left[ \begin{array}{c}{x}_{3} \\ - {\displaystyle \frac{1}{2}} {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{array} \right]},\qquad x_3 \in \mathbb{R}.
$$
Finally, for any $x_3 \neq 0,$ we obtain 

$$
\dfrac{x_2}{x_1}=\dfrac{\left( -\dfrac 12x_3\right)}{x_3}=-\dfrac 12.
$$

Since $\mathcal{B}$ is a basis, the following properties must hold:

- $\mathcal{B}$ is a maximally linearly independent set of vectors in $V,$ and

- $\mathcal{B}$ spans $V.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{b}_{2}+{x}_{2}(-{b}_{1})+{x}_{3}({b}_{3}+{b}_{1}) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

is equivalent to

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{b}_{2}+({x}_{3}-{x}_{2}){b}_{1}+{x}_{3}{b}_{3} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which, since $\left\{ \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3} \right\}$ is linearly independent, gives
$$
{\left\{  \begin{array}{l}{x}_{1} = 0 \\ {x}_{3} - {x}_{2} = 0 \\ {x}_{3} = 0\end{array} \right. }
	\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
	{\left\{  \begin{array}{l}{x}_{1} = 0 \\ {x}_{2} = 0 \\ {x}_{3} = 0.\end{array} \right. }
$$
Also, $\left\{ \mathbf{b_2},- \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_3}+\mathbf{b_1} \right\}$ spans $V$ since any linear combination of vectors from $\mathcal{B}$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\left\{ \mathbf{b_2},- \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_3}+\mathbf{b_1} \right\}\mathbin{:}$

$$
x_1\mathbf{b}_1+x_2\mathbf{b}_2+x_3\mathbf{b}_3
=
x_2\mathbf{b}_2+(x_3-x_1)(-\mathbf{b}_1)+x_3 (\mathbf{b_3}+\mathbf{b_1})
$$

- Statement II is false. In order for $\left\{ \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3}, \mathbf{0}  \right\}$ to span $V,$ every element of $\mathcal{B}$ must be able to be expressed as a linear combination of elements of $\left\{ \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3}, \mathbf{0}  \right\}.$ But the vector $\mathbf{b}_1 \in \mathcal{B}$ can't be written as a linear combination of the elements of $\left\{ \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3}, \mathbf{0}  \right\}.$

- Statement III is false. If $\left\{  -\mathbf{b_2}, 3\mathbf{b_1}\right\}$ is linearly dependent then there exist $x_1$ and $x_2$ not both zero such that

$$
x_1(-\mathbf{b_2}) + x_2(3\mathbf{b_1}) = \mathbf{0}.
$$

Then, we would have

$$
(3x_2) \cdot \mathbf{b_1} + (-x_1) \cdot \mathbf{b_2} + 0 \cdot \mathbf{b}_3= \mathbf{0}.
$$

But this would mean that $\mathcal{B} = \left\{ \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3} \right\}$ is linearly dependent, which contradicts the fact that $\mathcal{B}$ is a basis of $V.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

In expanded form, the matrix looks as follows:
$$

$$
\textrm{Im}(\mathbf{T}) = 
		\left\{ 
			\mathbf{b} \:|\: 
			{ {\mathbf{T} ( \mathbf{u} ) = \mathbf{b}} \text{ for some } {\mathbf{u}}}
		\right\}
$$

Notice that $\mathbf{0}$ is always in the image of a linear transformation since $\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{0})=\mathbf{0}.$

As an example, let's consider the linear transformation
$$
\mathbf{S}: {\left[ \begin{array}{c}x \\ y\end{array} \right]} \longrightarrow {\left[ \begin{array}{c}2 x + 4 y \\ 3 x + 6 y\end{array} \right]}.
$$

Notice that, for example, the vector $\mathbf b = [6,9]^T$ is in the image of the transformation $\mathbf{S}$ since there is another vector $\mathbf{u} = [1,1]^T$ such that $\mathbf{S}(\mathbf{u})=\mathbf{b}{:}$

$$
\mathbf{S} \bigg( \underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}1 \\ 1\end{array} \right]} }_{\mathbf{u}} \bigg) = {\left[ \begin{array}{c}2 \cdot  1 + 4 \cdot  1 \\ 3 \cdot  1 + 6 \cdot  1\end{array} \right]}
	=\underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}6 \\ 9\end{array} \right]}}_{\mathbf{b}}

One useful property of diagonalization is that it allows us to easily determine the power of a matrix.

As an example, we consider the $2\times 2$ matrix $A={\left[ \begin{array}{cc}1 & - 2 \\ 0 & - 1\end{array} \right]}$ with the diagonalization
$$
A =	\underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}5 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{array} \right]}}_{\large P}
		\underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}1 & 0 \\ 0 & - 1\end{array} \right]}}_{\large D}
		\underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}{\displaystyle \frac{1}{5}} & - {\displaystyle \frac{1}{5}} \\ 0 & 1\end{array} \right]}}_{\large P^{-1}}.
$$

We will use the diagonalization of $A$ to compute $A^{55}.$

Let's start by computing $A^2.$ Using the properties of matrix multiplication, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2} & =PD{P}^{-1}\cdot PD{P}^{-1} \\  & =PD\cancel{{P}^{-1}\cdot P}D{P}^{-1} \\  & =P(DD){P}^{-1} \\  & =P{D}^{2}{P}^{-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $A^3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{3} & ={A}^{2}\cdot A \\  & =P{D}^{2}{P}^{-1}\cdot PD{P}^{-1} \\  & =P{D}^{2}\cancel{{P}^{-1}\cdot P}D{P}^{-1} \\  & =P({D}^{2}D){P}^{-1} \\  & =P{D}^{3}{P}^{-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

We see that the matrix $P$ and its inverse $P^{-1}$ will always cancel each other out in the middle of the multiplication! So by induction, we have that

$$
A^{\color{blue}55}=P \cdot D^{\color{blue}55} \cdot P^{-1}.
$$

Now, we only need to find $D^{\color{blue}55}.$

Since $D$ is a diagonal matrix, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}^{2} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}{1}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & (-1)^{2}\end{bmatrix} \\ {D}^{3} & ={D}^{2}D=\begin{bmatrix}{1}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & (-1)^{2}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}{1}^{3} & 0 \\ 0 & (-1)^{3}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Following this pattern, we get

$$
D^{ {\color{blue}55}}	= {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}{1}^{ {\color{blue}55}} & 0 \\ 0 & ( - 1 {)}^{ {\color{blue}55}}\end{array} \right]}
						= {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}1 & 0 \\ 0 & - 1\end{array} \right]}.
$$

Therefore, we can conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{55} & =\begin{bmatrix}5 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}{\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}}^{55}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{5} & -\frac{1}{5} \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{5} & -\frac{1}{5} \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5 & -1 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{5} & -\frac{1}{5} \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In general, given that $A = PDP^{-1},$ for any non-negative integer ${\color{blue}k},$ we obtain 

$$
A^{\color{blue}k} = P \cdot D^{\color{blue}k} \cdot P^{-1}.
$$

Remember that the diagonalization of a $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ and corresponding linearly independent eigenvectors $\mathbf{v_1}$ and $\mathbf{v_2}$ is
$$
A=
	\underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}| & | \\ {\mathbf{v}}_{1} & {\mathbf{v}}_{2} \\ | & |\end{array} \right]}}_{P}
	\underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{array} \right]}}_{D}
	\underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}| & | \\ {\mathbf{v}}_{1} & {\mathbf{v}}_{2} \\ | & |\end{array} \right]}^{-1}}_{P^{-1}}.
$$

This idea also works in reverse. Given a diagonalization $A$ in the form 

$$
A=PDP^{-1},
$$

 

we can immediately deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are the diagonal entries of $D,$ and the corresponding eigenvectors are the columns of $P.$ This is because the diagonalization of a matrix is (almost) unique.

**Note:** The diagonalization is "almost" unique because the order of the eigenvalue-eigenvector pairs may vary, and the eigenvectors may be replaced with scalar multiples of themselves. However, none of these variations change the actual outcome regarding the eigenvalue-eigenvector pairs that we deduce.

In general, consider a basis $\mathcal{B}=\{ \mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2,\dots, \mathbf{b}_n \}$ of a vector space $V$ and a linear transformation $\mathbf{T}:V \rightarrow V$. For any $\mathbf{x}\in V$ we have that

$$
\mathbf{x} = x_1\mathbf{b}_1+x_2\mathbf{b}_2+\cdots + x_n\mathbf{b}_n
$$

or, equivalently $$
\displaystyle [\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}} = {\left[ \begin{array}{c}{x}_{1} \\ \vdots  \\ {x}_{n}\end{array} \right]}.
$$
Then the matrix for $\mathbf{T}$ relative to $\mathcal{B}$ is given by
$$
[\mathbf{T}]_{\mathcal{B}} =	{\left[ \begin{array}{cccc}| & | &  & | \\ [ \mathbf{T} ( {\mathbf{b}}_{1} ) {]}_{\mathcal{B}} & [ \mathbf{T} ( {\mathbf{b}}_{2} ) {]}_{\mathcal{B}} & \cdots  & [ \mathbf{T} ( {\mathbf{b}}_{n} ) {]}_{\mathcal{B}} \\ | & | &  & |\end{array} \right]}.
$$

Therefore
$$
[\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{x})]_{\mathcal{B}} = \underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{cccc}| & | &  & | \\ [ \mathbf{T} ( {\mathbf{b}}_{1} ) {]}_{\mathcal{B}} & [ \mathbf{T} ( {\mathbf{b}}_{2} ) {]}_{\mathcal{B}} & \cdots  & [ \mathbf{T} ( {\mathbf{b}}_{n} ) {]}_{\mathcal{B}} \\ | & | &  & |\end{array} \right]}}_{\large[\mathbf{T}]_{\mathcal{B}}}
	\underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ \vdots  \\ {x}_{n}\end{array} \right]}}_{[\large\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}}.
$$

We can use repeated matrix multiplication to determine the state of a system given its initial state and some information about how one state transitions to the next state. To explain this concretely, suppose we have a population where people live either in the city or the countryside. A study carried out by the local authority shows that, each year, - $6\%$ of the city population relocates to the countryside, - $3\%$ of the countryside population relocates to the city, and - everyone else remains where they are. This information can be represented using a diagram, like the one below. ![](images/ab/ab6b3cecac2af22b8665078db56c7daf492c0381434c9c88fe21f2630f743466.png) We can also present this information as a table:
From:
City Countryside
To: City $0.94$ $0.03$
Countryside $0.06$ $0.97$
We want to use this information to determine how the population will be distributed $n$ years after the study was carried out. First, let's turn this table into a matrix $P\mathbin{:}$ $$ P={\left[ \begin{array}{cc}0.94 & 0.03 \\ 0.06 & 0.97\end{array} \right]} $$ Notice that this matrix has the following properties: - it is a square matrix - the sum of the entries in each column equals $1$ - all entries in the matrix are non-negative A square matrix with these properties is called a **stochastic matrix**. Now suppose that, at the time of the study, $70\%$ of the population lived in the city and $30\%$ in the countryside. We can represent this **initial state** using a so-called **stochastic vector** $\mathbf x_0,$ given by $$ \mathbf{x}_0={\left[ \begin{array}{c}0.70 \\ 0.30\end{array} \right]}. $$ Stochastic vectors contain non-negative entries only, and the sum of the entries equals $1.$ Note that each column of $P$ is a stochastic vector. Now that we have our stochastic matrix and initial state vector, we can use matrix multiplication to calculate the population distribution sometime after the initial study took place: - To calculate the population distribution after one year, we calculate the product $P\mathbf x_0\mathbin{:}$ $$ P\mathbf{x}_0 = {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}0.94 & 0.03 \\ 0.06 & 0.97\end{array} \right]}{\left[ \begin{array}{c}0.70 \\ 0.30\end{array} \right]} = {\left[ \begin{array}{c}0.667 \\ 0.333\end{array} \right]} $$ The resulting vector $$ \mathbf{x}_1={\left[ \begin{array}{c}0.667 \\ 0.333\end{array} \right]} $$ tells us that one year after the study, $66.7$% of the population will live in the city, and $33.3$% will live in the countryside. - To model the distribution after $2$ years, we compute $P\mathbf x_1\mathbin{:}$ $$ P\mathbf{x}_1 = {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}0.94 & 0.03 \\ 0.06 & 0.97\end{array} \right]}{\left[ \begin{array}{c}0.667 \\ 0.333\end{array} \right]} = {\left[ \begin{array}{c}0.637 \\ 0.363\end{array} \right]} $$ The resulting vector $$ \mathbf{x}_2= {\left[ \begin{array}{c}0.637 \\ 0.363\end{array} \right]} $$ tells us that two years after the study, $63.7$% of the population will live in the city, and $36.3$% will live in the countryside.

Suppose that we have bases $\mathcal{B}=\{ \mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2 \}$ and $\mathcal{C}=\{ \mathbf{c}_1,\mathbf{c}_2 \},$ and we want to find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C},$ denoted $P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}}.$

Recall that the columns of $P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}}$ are the coordinates of the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C},$ that is
$$
P_{\small{\color{black}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{black}\mathcal{C}}}
	=
	\left[
	{\begin{array}{cc}| & | \\ [ {\color{black}{\mathbf{b}}_{1}} {]}_{ {\color{black}\mathcal{C}}} & [ {\color{black}{\mathbf{b}}_{2}} {]}_{ {\color{black}\mathcal{C}}} \\ | & |\end{array}}
	\right].
$$

To compute $P_{\small{\color{black}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{black}\mathcal{C}}},$ we need to find the coordinates of $\mathbf{b}_1$ and $\mathbf{b}_2$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix
$$
M =
	\left[
	{\begin{array}{cc|cc}| & | & | & | \\ {\mathbf{c}}_{1} & {\mathbf{c}}_{2} & {\mathbf{b}}_{1} & {\mathbf{b}}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{array}}
	\right].
$$

If we reduce the left-hand side of $M$ to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination, $P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}}$ will emerge on the right-hand side:

$$
M \sim
	\left[
	{\begin{array}{c|c}I & {P}_{\mathcal{B} \to  \mathcal{C}}\end{array}}
	\right].
$$

The structure $\mathbb{R}^n$ is called a **vector space**. However, many other structures possess properties similar to $\mathbb{R}^n.$ These other structures can be called vector spaces too. 

In this lesson, we'll learn about some important properties used to construct vector spaces. We begin by discussing what it means for a set to be **closed** under addition and scalar multiplication.

As an example, consider the set $\mathrm{M}_2(\mathbb{R})$ of all $2 \times 2$ matrices with real entries:

$$
\mathrm{M}_2(\mathbb{R}) = 
	\left\{
		{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}a & b \\ c & d\end{array} \right]} \: : \: a,b,c,d \in \mathbb{R}
	\right\}
$$

For this set of matrices, we can define two operations:

- the addition of two matrices, and

- the multiplication of a matrix by a real number (called a scalar).

Now, notice the following:

- $\mathrm{M}_2(\mathbb{R})$ is **closed under addition**. This means that the sum of *any* two matrices from $\mathrm{M}_2(\mathbb{R})$ is also a matrix in $\mathrm{M}_2(\mathbb{R}).$

- $\mathrm{M}_2(\mathbb{R})$ is **closed under scalar multiplication**. This means that the product of *any* scalar and *any* matrix from $\mathrm{M}_2(\mathbb{R})$ is also a matrix in $\mathrm{M}_2(\mathbb{R}).$

Identifying that a set is closed under addition and scalar multiplication is an essential first step in determining whether a set can form a vector space.

A square matrix $A$ is called **diagonalizable** if there exists a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that

$$
A = PDP^{-1}.
$$

So, to **diagonalize** a matrix $A,$ we need to find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ that satisfy the equation above.

For example, let's diagonalize the matrix $A,$ given by

$$
A={\left[ \begin{array}{cc}0 & - 6 \\ 1 & 5\end{array} \right]}.
$$

To diagonalize a $2\times 2$ matrix, we follow a three-step **diagonalization algorithm.**

**Step 1:** Find the eigenvalues of the matrix.

We solve the characteristic equation $\vert A - \lambda I \vert = 0.$ For the given matrix, the eigenvalues are $\color{red}\lambda_1 =2$ and $\color{blue}\lambda_2 =3.$

**Step 2:** Find a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ consisting of eigenvectors of the matrix.

Following the usual method for computing eigenvectors, we get 

$$
{\color{red}\mathbf{v_1}}={\color{red}{\left[ \begin{array}{c}3 \\ - 1\end{array} \right]}}
	\qquad\textrm{and}\qquad
	{\color{blue}\mathbf{v_2}}={\color{blue}{\left[ \begin{array}{c}- 2 \\ 1\end{array} \right]}}
$$

corresponding to the eigenvalues $\color{red}\lambda_1 =2$ and $\color{blue}\lambda_2 =3,$ respectively.

Note that $\left\{ {\color{red}\mathbf{v_1}}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{v_2}}\right\}$ is a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ since eigenvectors corresponding to distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent. This becomes important later.

**Step 3: ** Construct the matrices $D$ and $P.$

Now that we have our eigenvalues and corresponding eigenvectors, we can construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and invertible matrix $P.$

The matrix $D$ has the eigenvalues of the matrix as its entries on the diagonal. For now, we can write them in any order. So, we let

$$
D= {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}{\color{red}2} & 0 \\ 0 & {\color{blue}3}\end{array} \right]}.
$$

Then, the columns of $P$ are the corresponding eigenvectors. We need to write each eigenvector in the *same* column as its respective eigenvalue in the matrix $D.$ So, we get

$$
P={\left[ \begin{array}{cc}{\color{red}3} & {\color{blue}- 2} \\ {\color{red}- 1} & {\color{blue}1}\end{array} \right]}.
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A=PD{P}^{-1} & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}{\begin{bmatrix}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can check our solution by computing the product on the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}{\begin{bmatrix}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}}^{-1} & =\begin{bmatrix}6 & -6 \\ -2 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & -6 \\ 1 & 5\end{bmatrix} \\  & =A\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

There is a theorem that states the following:

*If $A$ is a $2 \times 2$ matrix, then it is diagonalizable if and only if there exists a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ that consists of eigenvectors of $A.$*

We can break this down into two possible cases:

- If $A$ has two distinct eigenvalues, then it is indeed diagonalizable. This is because two distinct eigenvalues will give rise to two linearly independent eigenvectors (one for each eigenvalue). 

So, for a matrix $A$ with eigenvalues $\color{red}\lambda_1$ and $\color{blue}\lambda_2$ and corresponding eigenvectors $\color{red}\mathbf{v_1}$ and $\color{blue}\mathbf{v_2},$ we have
$$
A=
	\underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}{\color{red}|} & {\color{blue}|} \\ {\color{red}{\mathbf{v}}_{\mathbf{1}}} & {\color{blue}{\mathbf{v}}_{\mathbf{2}}} \\ {\color{red}|} & {\color{blue}|}\end{array} \right]}}_{P}
	\underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}{\color{red}{\lambda }_{1}} & 0 \\ 0 & {\color{blue}{\lambda }_{2}}\end{array} \right]}}_{D}
	{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}{\color{red}|} & {\color{blue}|} \\ {\color{red}{\mathbf{v}}_{\mathbf{1}}} & {\color{blue}{\mathbf{v}}_{\mathbf{2}}} \\ {\color{red}|} & {\color{blue}|}\end{array} \right]}^{-1}.
$$

- If we get a double root $\lambda$ of the characteristic equation, the matrix will be diagonalizable *only if* we can find exactly two linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda,$ which may or may not be possible. Another way of saying this is that the corresponding eigenspace $V_\lambda$ must be of dimension $2.$

Up to now, we've been using the following formulas:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{r} & ={f}_{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{f}_{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ {f}_{\theta } & =-r{f}_{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +r{f}_{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

We can treat the above as a system of equations in the "unknowns" $f_x$ and $f_y.$ Solving this system gives explicit expressions for $f_x$ and $f_y$ in terms of functions of $r$ and $\theta.$

For example, suppose we want an explicit formula for $f_x.$ We can eliminate $f_y$ by multiplying the first equation by $r\cos\theta$ and the second equation by $\sin\theta$ to give

$$
\begin{aligned}r{f}_{r}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =r{f}_{x}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +r{f}_{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ {f}_{\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =-r{f}_{x}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +r{f}_{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Subtracting the second equation from the first gives

$$
r f_r \cos\theta - f_\theta \sin\theta = r f_x(\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta),
$$

which simplifies to

$$
f_x = f_r \cos\theta - \dfrac1r f_\theta \sin\theta.
$$

We can use a similar procedure to write $f_y$ in terms of functions of $r$ and $\theta.$ Our results as summarized below:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x} &= \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial r} \cos \theta
						-\dfrac{1}{r} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial \theta}\sin \theta\\[1ex]
\dfrac {\partial f}{\partial y} &= \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial r} \sin \theta
						+ \dfrac{1}{r} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial \theta}\cos \theta
\end{aligned}
$$

A square matrix $A$ is diagonalizable if there exists a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that

$$
A = PDP^{-1}.
$$

So, diagonalizing $A$ means finding matrices $D$ and $P$ that satisfy this equation. 

For example, let's diagonalize the matrix $A,$ given by

$$
A={\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}- 1 & - 3 & 6 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ - 1 & - 1 & 4\end{array} \right]}.
$$

To diagonalize a $3 \times 3$ matrix, we follow a three-step **diagonalization algorithm.**

**Step 1:** Find the eigenvalues of the matrix.

We solve the characteristic equation $\vert A - \lambda I \vert = 0.$ For the given matrix, the eigenvalues are 

$$
{\color{red}{\lambda_1}} = {\color{red}{\lambda_2}} = {\color{red}2}\qquad \textrm{and} \qquad{\color{blue}\lambda_3 =1}.
$$

**Step 2:** Find a basis (if it exists) consisting of eigenvectors of the matrix.

Following the usual method for computing eigenvectors, we get 

$$
{\color{red}\mathbf{v}_1}={\color{red}{\left[ \begin{array}{c}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{array} \right]}}, \qquad
	{\color{red}\mathbf{v}_2}={\color{red}{\left[ \begin{array}{c}- 1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{array} \right]}},
	\qquad\textrm{and}\qquad
	{\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_3}={\color{blue}{\left[ \begin{array}{c}3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{array} \right]}}
$$

corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\color{red}{\lambda_1}} = {\color{red}{\lambda_2}} = {\color{red}2}$ and ${\color{blue}\lambda_3 =1},$ respectively.

**Watch out!** In this example, the total number of linearly independent eigenvectors equals the number of rows/columns of the matrix. If we obtain fewer eigenvectors at this step, then the matrix is *not* diagonalizable.

**Step 3: ** Construct the matrices $D$ and $P.$

Now that we have our eigenvalues and corresponding eigenvectors, we can construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and invertible matrix $P.$

The matrix $D$ has the eigenvalues of the matrix as its entries on the main diagonal. We can write them in any order, so we let

$$

Suppose that we have a straight line passing through the point $P(3,-1,7)$ and that's parallel to the direction vector $\mathbf{v}={\left[ \begin{array}{c}0 \\ 5 \\ - 3\end{array} \right]}.$ As we know, we can write the vector equation of the line as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =p+tv \\ r & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -1 \\ 7\end{bmatrix}+t\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 5 \\ -3\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

where $t \in (-\infty,\infty).$

Using the vector equation above, we can create a set of **parametric equations** where we express a general point $(x,y,z)$ in terms of  the parameter $t.$

If we let $\mathbf{r}={\left[ \begin{array}{c}x \\ y \\ z\end{array} \right]}$ be the position vector of the general point $(x,y,z),$ then the above equation can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -1 \\ 7\end{bmatrix}+t\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 5 \\ -3\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -1 \\ 7\end{bmatrix}+t\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 5 \\ -3\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -1+5t \\ 7-3t\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following system of equations:
$$
\left\{
	{\begin{array}{l}x = 3 \\ y = - 1 + 5 t \\ z = 7 - 3 t\end{array}}
	\right.
$$

The equations in the above system are called the **parametric equations** of the straight line.
Geometrically, the equation states that a point belongs to the line if and only if its coordinates have the form

$$
(3, \: -1+5t, \: 7-3t),
$$

where $t \in (-\infty, \infty).$

$$

where $P_{\small{\mathcal{B}}\to{\mathcal{C}}}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}.$

First, let's denote the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$ as $\{ \mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2 \}$ and $\{ \mathbf{c}_1,\mathbf{c}_2 \}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of vectors from $\mathcal{B}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of $\mathbf{b}_1$ and $\mathbf{b}_2$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}.$ To do this, we consider the matrix

$$
M =

	{\begin{array}{cc|cc}| & | & | & | \\ {\mathbf{c}}_{1} & {\mathbf{c}}_{2} & {\mathbf{b}}_{1} & {\mathbf{b}}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{array}}
	\right].
$$

We reduce $M$ using Gaussian elimination until we get the identity matrix on the left. By doing this, we obtain the required change-of-coordinates matrix on the right.

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & -1 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,
$$
P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}} =

Now, we compute the inverse of $P_{\small{\mathcal{B}}\to{\mathcal{C}}} \mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C}^{-1} & ={\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{1\cdot 1-0\cdot (-1)}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can compute the matrix of $\mathbf{T}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C} \mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & -3 \\ 2 & 6\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & -9 \\ 2 & 6\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & -7 \\ 2 & 8\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

$$

So, the natural question now is, how does a rotation-scaling matrix 
$$
A={\left[ \begin{array}{cc}{\color{blue}a} & - {\color{red}b} \\ {\color{red}b} & {\color{blue}a}\end{array} \right]}

relate to the individual rotation and scaling matrices?

First, setting the two equal to each other, we get

$$
{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}{\color{blue}a} & - {\color{red}b} \\ {\color{red}b} & {\color{blue}a}\end{array} \right]}
=
{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}r & 0 \\ 0 & r\end{array} \right]}{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}\cos   \theta  & - \sin   \theta  \\ \sin   \theta  & \cos   \theta \end{array} \right]}.
$$

From this, we can find the scale factor and angle of rotation of a rotation-scaling matrix. First, notice that we have

$$
{\color{blue}a} = {\color{blue}r\cos\theta}, \quad \textrm{and}\quad {\color{red}b} = {\color{red}r\sin\theta}.
$$

To find $r$ in terms of $a$ and $b,$ we can square and then add the two equations above. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}^{2}+{b}^{2} & ={r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & ={r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & ={r}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the scale factor $r$ is given by

$$
r = \sqrt{a^2+b^2} = \sqrt{\det{A}}.
$$

Similarly, to find the rotation angle $\theta$ in terms of $a$ and $b,$ we start with the equations

$$
{\color{blue}a} = {\color{blue}r\cos\theta}, \quad \textrm{and}\quad {\color{red}b} = {\color{red}r\sin\theta}.
$$

Dividing the second equation by the first, we get

$$
\tan\theta = \dfrac{b}{a}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \theta = \arctan\left(\dfrac ba \right).
$$

It's also possible to recover both the original scaling *and* rotation matrix once the scale factor $r$ is known. Let's see how that works.

For any point on the unit circle, we can draw a right triangle whose hypotenuse is the line segment between the origin and the point.

![](images/b1/b1ec08957fd0d09179853d6d56c20b7058c4531bdd7e766c5b3462ba246fce2b.png)

Each hypotenuse is the radius of the unit circle and consequently has a length equal to $1.$

Therefore, the coordinates of *any* point on the unit circle must satisfy the Pythagorean theorem:

$$
x^2+y^2=1.
$$

We can use this fact to find one coordinate of a point on the unit circle given the other.

For example, suppose that the $x$-coordinate of the point $A$ in the fourth quadrant on the unit circle is $\dfrac{3}{7}.$ To find the $y$-coordinate, we substitute $x=\dfrac{3}{7}$ into the above and solve for $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
		x^2+y^2&=1\\[5pt]
	          \left(\dfrac{3}{7}\right)^2+y^2&=1\\[5pt]
		\dfrac{9}{49}+y^2&=1\\[5pt]
		y^2&= 1-\dfrac{9}{49}\\[5pt]
		y^2&= \dfrac{40}{49}\\[5pt]
		y&= \sqrt{\dfrac{40}{49}}\\[5pt]
	        y &= \pm \dfrac{2\sqrt{10}}{7}

\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ lies in the *fourth* quadrant, $y$ must be *negative*. So we select the negative answer. Therefore, $y=-\dfrac{2\sqrt{10}}{7}.$

Rotation-scaling matrices are involved in an important theorem regarding complex eigenvalues.

To sketch out the key idea, let's consider the matrix 

$$
A={\left[ \begin{array}{cc}- 5 & - 10 \\ 4 & 7\end{array} \right]},
$$

which has the complex eigenvalue 

$$
\lambda=1-2\textrm{i}={\color{blue}1}+({\color{red}-2})\textrm{i}
$$

and the corresponding complex eigenvector 

$$
\mathbf{v}
={\left[ \begin{array}{c}2 - \text{i} \\ - 1 + \text{i}\end{array} \right]}
={\left[ \begin{array}{c}{\color{blue}2} + ( {\color{red}- 1} ) \text{i} \\ {\color{blue}- 1} + {\color{red}1} \text{i}\end{array} \right]}.
$$

Now, we construct a rotation-scaling matrix $C$ using the real and imaginary parts of the eigenvalue $\lambda$ as follows:
$$
C =	{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}{\color{blue}\text{Re} (} \lambda  {\color{blue})} & {\color{red}\text{Im} (} \lambda  {\color{red})} \\ - {\color{red}\text{Im} (} \lambda  {\color{red})} & {\color{blue}\text{Re} (} \lambda  {\color{blue})}\end{array} \right]}
		={\left[ \begin{array}{cc}{\color{blue}1} & {\color{red}- 2} \\ {\color{red}2} & {\color{blue}1}\end{array} \right]}
$$
We also construct a matrix $P$ whose columns are the real and imaginary parts of the corresponding eigenvector:
$$
P =	{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}{\color{blue}|} & {\color{red}|} \\ {\color{blue}\text{Re} (} \mathbf{v} {\color{blue})} & {\color{red}\text{Im} (} \mathbf{v} {\color{red})} \\ {\color{blue}|} & {\color{red}|}\end{array} \right]}
		={\left[ \begin{array}{cc}{\color{blue}2} & {\color{red}- 1} \\ {\color{blue}- 1} & {\color{red}1}\end{array} \right]}.
$$

The **rotation-scaling theorem** states that $A$ can be factored as follows:

$$
A=PCP^{-1}
$$

 

Let's check that this is true in this case:

$$
\begin{aligned}PC{P}^{-1} & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}{\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}}^{-1} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & -5 \\ 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-5 & -10 \\ 4 & 7\end{bmatrix} \\  & =A\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Let's now formally state the rotation-scaling theorem:

*Let $A$ be a $2 \times 2$ matrix with real entries. If $\lambda$ is a complex (not real) eigenvalue of $A,$ and $\mathbf{v}$ is an eigenvector corresponding to $\lambda,$ then *

$$
A = PCP^{-1}
$$

*where*
$$
P= {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}| & | \\ \text{Re} ( \mathbf{v} ) & \text{Im} ( \mathbf{v} ) \\ | & |\end{array} \right]} ,\qquad
	C= {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}\text{Re} ( \lambda  ) & \text{Im} ( \lambda  ) \\ - \text{Im} ( \lambda  ) & \text{Re} ( \lambda  )\end{array} \right]}.
$$

Note the following:

- When two matrices $A$ and $C$ are related via the equation $A = PCP^{-1},$ we say that they are **similar.**

- The rotation-scaling theorem tells us that every $2 \!\times\! 2$ real matrix with complex (non-real) eigenvalues is similar to a rotation-scaling matrix.

- We call the right-hand side of $A = PCP^{-1}$ the **rotation-scaling form** of $A.$ We can also refer to this as the **rotation-scaling decomposition** of $A.$

- The matrix $P$ *must* be constructed from the eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue defined by $C.$

We have the following theorem regarding the block diagonalization of a real $3\!\times\! 3$ matrix:

*If $A$ is a real $3\times 3$ matrix with one real eigenvalue ${\color{red}\lambda_1}$ with corresponding eigenvector ${\color{red}{\mathbf{v}_1}},$ and two complex eigenvalues ${\color{blue}\lambda_2} = \overline{\color{blue}\lambda}_{\color{blue}3}$ with corresponding eigenvectors ${\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2} = \overline{\color{blue}\mathbf{v}}_{\color{blue}3},$ then* 

$$
A=PBP^{-1},
$$

*where the matrices $B$ and $P$ are given by*
$$
B=
	\left[{\begin{array}{c|cc}{\color{red}{\lambda }_{1}} & 0 & 0 \\ \hline 0 & {\color{blue}\text{Re} ( {\lambda }_{2} )} & {\color{blue}\text{Im} ( {\lambda }_{2} )} \\ 0 & {\color{blue}- \text{Im} ( {\lambda }_{2} )} & {\color{blue}\text{Re} ( {\lambda }_{2} )}\end{array}}\right], \qquad 
	P=
	{\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}{\color{red}|} & {\color{blue}|} & {\color{blue}|} \\ {\color{red}{\mathbf{v}}_{1}} & {\color{blue}\text{Re} ( {\mathbf{v}}_{2} )} & {\color{blue}\text{Im} ( {\mathbf{v}}_{2} )} \\ {\color{red}|} & {\color{blue}|} & {\color{blue}|}\end{array} \right]}.
$$

In other words, if $A$ is a real $3\!\times\! 3$ matrix with one real eigenvalue and two complex eigenvalues, then $A$ is block diagonalizable.

Note the following:

- The block of $B$ constructed from the real and imaginary parts of $\color{blue}\lambda_2$ is a rotation-scaling matrix.

Scaling matrices are of the form
$$

The scaling matrix $S$ scales a vector by a scale factor of $r,$ where the origin is the center of enlargement.

A **unit vector** is a vector whose length is equal to $1.$ If we divide a *non-zero* vector $\mathbf{x}$ by its norm $\Vert \mathbf{x} \Vert,$ we obtain a unit vector $\mathbf{v}=\dfrac{\mathbf{x}}{\Vert\mathbf{x}\Vert},$ since

$$
\Vert \mathbf{v} \Vert	=\left\Vert \dfrac{\mathbf{x}}{\Vert \mathbf{x} \Vert} \right\Vert
						= \dfrac{1}{\Vert \mathbf{x} \Vert}\cdot\Vert \mathbf{x} \Vert
						= 1.
$$

The process of dividing a vector $\mathbf{x}$ by its norm $\Vert \mathbf{x} \Vert$ is called **normalizing the vector $\mathbf{x}.$** We say that the unit vector $\mathbf{v}=\dfrac{\mathbf{x}}{\Vert\mathbf{x}\Vert}$ is *in the same direction* as $\mathbf{x}.$

We've already seen how to find the orthogonal projection of a vector onto a subspace in the case when the subspace is defined using an orthogonal basis. In this lesson, we'll learn how to do the same thing in the case of non-orthogonal bases.

For example, consider the following vectors:
$$
\mathbf{a}_1={\left[ \begin{array}{c}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{array} \right]}, \:
	\mathbf{a}_2={\left[ \begin{array}{c}1 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{array} \right]}, 
	\qquad
	\mathbf{x}={\left[ \begin{array}{c}2 \\ 4 \\ 0\end{array} \right]}
$$
How can we find the orthogonal projection $\mathbf{x}_S$ of the vector $\mathbf{x}$ onto the subspace $S = \textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \}?$ Notice that since $\mathbf a_1\cdot \mathbf a_2 \neq 0,$ the vectors $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2$ are not orthogonal.

As usual, we would like to write $\mathbf{x}$ as 

$$
\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x}_S + \mathbf{x}_{S^\perp},
$$

where $\mathbf{x}_S = k_1 \mathbf{a}_1 + k_2 \mathbf{a}_2 \in S$ and $\mathbf{x}_{S^\perp} \!\in S^\perp.$

![](images/3a/3a5576fcaf9e0be6fc14978eb91dcbaceee75cbfddaa537fdb05d34b8e31e2e0.png)

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{{S}^{⊥}} & =x-{x}_{S} \\  & =x-({k}_{1}{a}_{1}+{k}_{2}{a}_{2}) \\  & =x-{k}_{1}{a}_{1}-{k}_{2}{a}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\mathbf{x}_{S^\perp} \in S^\perp,$ that is, $\mathbf{x}_{S^\perp} \perp S,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{{S}^{⊥}}⊥{a}_{1} \\ {x}_{{S}^{⊥}}⊥{a}_{2}\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{{S}^{⊥}}\cdot {a}_{1} &=0 \\ {x}_{{S}^{⊥}}\cdot {a}_{2} &=0.\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute the expression for $\mathbf{x}_{S^\perp}$ into the system to get
$$
{\left\{  \begin{array}{l}( \mathbf{x} - {k}_{1} {\mathbf{a}}_{1} - {k}_{2} {\mathbf{a}}_{2} ) \cdot  {\mathbf{a}}_{1} = 0 \\ ( \mathbf{x} - {k}_{1} {\mathbf{a}}_{1} - {k}_{2} {\mathbf{a}}_{2} ) \cdot  {\mathbf{a}}_{2} = 0\end{array} \right. }
	\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
	{\left\{  \begin{array}{l}{k}_{1} {\color{blue}( {\mathbf{a}}_{1} \cdot  {\mathbf{a}}_{1} )} + {k}_{2} {\color{blue}( {\mathbf{a}}_{2} \cdot  {\mathbf{a}}_{1} )} = {\color{red}( \mathbf{x} \cdot  {\mathbf{a}}_{1} )} \\ {k}_{1} {\color{blue}( {\mathbf{a}}_{1} \cdot  {\mathbf{a}}_{2} )} + {k}_{2} {\color{blue}( {\mathbf{a}}_{2} \cdot  {\mathbf{a}}_{2} )} = {\color{red}( \mathbf{x} \cdot  {\mathbf{a}}_{2} )} .\end{array} \right. }
$$

We can write this system in an equivalent matrix form as follows:
$$
{\color{blue}
	{\left[ \begin{array}{c}- \hspace{0.222em} \hspace{0.222em} {\mathbf{a}}_{1} \hspace{0.222em} \hspace{0.222em} - \\ - \hspace{0.222em} \hspace{0.222em} {\mathbf{a}}_{2} \hspace{0.222em} \hspace{0.222em} -\end{array} \right]}
	{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}| & | \\ {\mathbf{a}}_{1} & {\mathbf{a}}_{2} \\ | & |\end{array} \right]}
}
	{\left[ \begin{array}{c}{k}_{1} \\ {k}_{2}\end{array} \right]}
	=
{\color{red}
	{\left[ \begin{array}{c}- \hspace{0.222em} \hspace{0.222em} {\mathbf{a}}_{1} \hspace{0.222em} \hspace{0.222em} - \\ - \hspace{0.222em} \hspace{0.222em} {\mathbf{a}}_{2} \hspace{0.222em} \hspace{0.222em} -\end{array} \right]}
	{\left[ \begin{array}{c}| \\ \mathbf{x} \\ |\end{array} \right]}
}
$$

If we denote 
$$
A={\left[ \begin{array}{cc}| & | \\ {\mathbf{a}}_{1} & {\mathbf{a}}_{2} \\ | & |\end{array} \right]}
$$
and $\mathbf{k}={\left[ \begin{array}{c}{k}_{1} \\ {k}_{2}\end{array} \right]},$ then we obtain

$$
A^TA\mathbf{k} = A^T\mathbf{x}
	\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
	\mathbf{k}=(A^TA)^{-1}A^T\mathbf{x}.
$$

Also, we note that  $\mathbf{x}_S = k_1 \mathbf{a}_1 + k_2 \mathbf{a}_2$ can be expressed as $\textrm{proj}_{S}\,\mathbf{x}	= A\mathbf{k}.$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =Ak \\  & =A({A}^{T}A)^{-1}{A}^{T}x.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a formula for the orthogonal projection!

Now, we return to our example. Using the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot {(\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix})}^{-1}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 4 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot {(\begin{bmatrix}6 & 8 \\ 8 & 11\end{bmatrix})}^{-1}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}10 \\ 14\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}11 & -8 \\ -8 & 6\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}10 \\ 14\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Note**: Pay attention to the order in which we carried out the multiplication. Carrying out the operations in the order shown above can save us a lot of work!

If $\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 , \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n \}$ is a set of *linearly independent* vectors, then the orthogonal projection of a vector $\mathbf{x}$ onto the subspace $S = \textrm{span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 , \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n \}$ is given by

$$
\textrm{proj}_{S} \: \mathbf{x} = A(A^T\!A)^{-1}\!A^T\,\mathbf{x},
$$

 
where $A$ is the matrix whose columns are the vectors of $\mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 , \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n,$ that is,
$$
A = 
	{\left[ \begin{array}{cccc}| & | & \ldots  & | \\ {\mathbf{a}}_{1} & {\mathbf{a}}_{2} & \ldots  & {\mathbf{a}}_{n} \\ | & | & \ldots  & |\end{array} \right]}.
$$

**Watch out!** The fact that $\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 , \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n \}$ must be linearly independent is important. If the vectors are linearly dependent, we need to find the basis of the span before applying the formula.

The **Gram-Schmidt process** is an algorithm that we can use to construct an *orthogonal* basis if we are given a non-orthogonal basis to start with.

For example, consider the basis $\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \}$ for the subspace $V=\textrm{Span} \{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \},$ where
$$
\mathbf{a}_1 = {\left[ \begin{array}{c}1 \\ - 1\end{array} \right]},
	\qquad
	\mathbf{a}_2 = {\left[ \begin{array}{c}4 \\ 6\end{array} \right]}.
$$

We can use the above basis to construct an *orthogonal* basis for the given $2$-dimensional subspace. To do this, we use the Gram-Schmidt process, which involves $2$ steps:

- **Step 1:** Set ${\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_1}=\mathbf{a}_1.$

- **Step 2:** Find a vector $\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2$ in $V$ that's orthogonal to $\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_1.$ This can be achieved by computing

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}\,-\,{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{1}}\,{a}_{2} \\  & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

![](images/67/678cc056e3c9d3fbf17423ac591b3e85d84ee8060c0637840fe1c4c9e87aa878.png)

Notice that $\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2$ is written as a linear combination of $\mathbf{a}_1(={\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_1})$ and $\mathbf{a}_2.$ So this means that ${\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2} \in V,$ and also ${\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2} \perp {\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_1}.$
Moreover, 

$$
\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2\} = V = \textrm{Span}\{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2} \}.
$$

After applying the Gram-Schmidt process, we get the set $\mathcal{B}=\{{\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2}\},$ which is an orthogonal basis for $V.$

So, in our example, we start by setting $\mathbf{v}_1=\mathbf{a}_1={\left[ \begin{array}{c}1 \\ - 1\end{array} \right]}.$ Then, we find the vector $\mathbf{v}_2$ that's orthogonal to $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{v}_1\}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1} \\  & ={a}_{2}-\frac{4\cdot 1+6\cdot (-1)}{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}{v}_{1} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}-(-1)\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $$
\displaystyle \mathcal{B}=\{\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2\} = \left\{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}1 \\ - 1\end{array} \right]}, {\left[ \begin{array}{c}5 \\ 5\end{array} \right]} \right\}
$$ is an orthogonal basis for $V.$

Given a basis $\{\mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2\}$ for a subspace $V,$ we can use the Gram-Schmidt process to find an *orthonormal* basis of the subspace.

To do this, we simply execute the Gram-Schmidt process as before to obtain an orthogonal basis $\{\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2\},$ and then we normalize each vector in this basis to get the orthonormal basis $\{\mathbf{u}_1, \mathbf{u}_2\},$ where

$$
\mathbf{u}_1 = \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_1}{\Vert \mathbf{v}_1 \Vert},
	\quad
	\mathbf{u}_2 = \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_2}{\Vert \mathbf{v}_2 \Vert}.
$$

Consider the following data set:

| $x$ | **$100$** | **$110$** | **$120$** | **$130$** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $y$ | $12$ | $11$ | $12$ | $15$ |

Our goal is to describe how to use matrices to carry out a linear regression. That is, we want to find an equation of the form

$$
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x
$$

that best fits the given data points. 

![](images/8e/8ec830e3cf6154675487536afc0e09a42226eb83187b90238a0bfdcefeae5b38.png)

Let's write our problem in matrix notation. Substituting the values of $x$ into the regression equation and equating the results to the corresponding observed values of $y,$ we obtain the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{\beta }_{0}+100{\beta }_{1}=12 \\ {\beta }_{0}+110{\beta }_{1}=11 \\ {\beta }_{0}+120{\beta }_{1}=12 \\ {\beta }_{0}+130{\beta }_{1}=15\end{aligned}
$$

which can be expressed in matrix notation as

$$
\overbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}1 & 100 \\ 1 & 110 \\ 1 & 120 \\ 1 & 130\end{array} \right]}}^{X}
	\overbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}{\beta }_{0} \\ {\beta }_{1}\end{array} \right]}}^{𝜷}
	=
	\overbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}12 \\ 11 \\ 12 \\ 15\end{array} \right]}}^{\mathbf{y}}.
$$

The matrix $X$ is called the **design matrix,** and $\mathbf{y}$ is called the **observation vector**. 

Since our points do not lie on a straight line, there will be no parameters $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$ such that this equation is true. So instead, we seek parameters $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$ that best approximate the solution.

In other words, we seek to find a column vector $\boldsymbol\beta$ such that

$$
\| \mathbf{y} - X\boldsymbol{\beta}\|
$$

is as small as possible.

Notice that this is exactly the least-squares problem for the system $X \boldsymbol{\beta} = \mathbf{y}.$ Therefore, the coefficients of the line that best fits the data can be found as the solution to the corresponding least-squares problem! 

This approach to finding parameters for a linear regression model is often called **ordinary least squares (OLS) regression**.

Pre-multiplying the equation $X \boldsymbol{\beta} = \mathbf{y}$ by $X^T,$ we obtain the corresponding normal equation

$$
X^T \! X {\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}} = X^T \mathbf{y}.
$$

Since the columns of $X$ are linearly independent, the matrix ${X^T}X$ is invertible, and 

$$
{\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}} = (X^T \! X )^{-1} X^T \mathbf{y}.
$$

Substituting $X$ and $\mathbf{y}$ into the formula above and simplifying, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\hat{\beta }=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0.1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the line of best fit (regression line) is 

$$
y = 1+ 0.1x.
$$

We've seen how to construct a simple linear regression model given some bivariate data $(x,y).$ We can generalize this technique to fit data to an arbitrary polynomial. We call this process **polynomial regression**.

In some cases, we might need to constrain the regression curve so that some of its coefficients equal zero.

It's known that the profit equals zero when the company does not produce any goods, so $y=0$ when $x=0.$ The company wishes to find a *quadratic* curve that best fits the data *subject to* the constraint that it should pass through the point $(0,0).$

So, our regression curve must pass through the point $(0,0).$ In other words, the $y$-intercept of the quadratic curve must be $0.$ Therefore, we want to find the quadratic function

where $X$ is the design matrix, $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ is the parameter vector, and $\mathbf{y}$ is the observation vector. 

The rest of the arguments are the same as before. Since our points do not lie on a quadratic curve, there will be no parameters $\beta_1$ and $\beta_2$ such that this equation is true. So instead, we seek parameters $\beta_1$ and $\beta_2$ that best approximate the solution.

First, notice that $10$ on the right-hand side has a block of $1$ zero:
$1 \!\!\!\!\!\!\!\underset{\substack{\uparrow \[2pt] \large \text{one zero}}}{\color{blue}0}\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!$

The Wronskian $W(y_1,y_2)$ of two functions $y_1(x)$ and $y_2(x)$ is defined as

$$
W(y_1,y_2) = 	
\left|
		{\begin{array}{cc}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{\prime } & {y}_{2}^{\prime }\end{array}}
	\right|	
= y_1 y_2'-  y_2 y_1'.
$$

In our case, we have $y_1(x) = 2x$ and $y_2(x) = x^2.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =2x{({x}^{2})}^{′}-{x}^{2}{(2x)}^{′} \\  & =4{x}^{2}-2{x}^{2} \\  & =2{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Suppose the functions $y_1(x)$ and $y_2(x)$ are defined on some interval $I.$
The Wronskian $W(y_1,y_2)$ of these functions is defined as

= y_1y_2'- y_2 y_1'.
$$

Recall the following:

- If $W \neq 0$ for at least one $x \in I,$ then $y_1$ and $y_2$ are linearly independent.

- If $W = 0$ and it’s known that $y_1$ and $y_2$ are solutions to the same second-order linear differential equation, then $y_1$ and $y_2$ are linearly dependent.

$$

which is nonzero for at least one $x \in \mathbb{R}.$

Therefore, the set $\left\{ y_1(x), y_2(x) \right\}$ is linearly independent on $\mathbb R.$

Therefore, we can write

$$
\textrm{Col}(A) = \textrm{Span}\,\mathcal B
= \textrm{Span}\{\mathbf a_1, \mathbf a_2\}

= 
\textrm{Span} \Bigg\{ 
		{\left[ \begin{array}{c}1 \\ 3\end{array} \right]},

If $Y =1-3X,$ then what is the probability density function of $Y?$

To compute the probability density function of a random variable $Y,$ where $Y = u(X)$ is a continuous, strictly monotonic function of a continuous random variable $X,$ we follow two steps:

- First, we find an expression for $F_Y$ terms of $F_X,$ where $F_Y$ and $F_X$ are the cumulative distribution functions of $Y$ and $X,$ respectively.

- Then, we differentiate $F_Y$ to get the probability density function $f_Y.$

Before we start, note that $Y = 1-3X$ is a strictly decreasing function of $X.$  Moreover, for $0 < x < 1,$ we have $-2 \lt y \lt 1 .$

![](images/3b/3bb641b1920d0ded33e4ffa25f3e0af856550dd3820edf30416bd79c3a6da264.png)

Now, using the definition of the cumulative distribution of $Y,$ for $-2 \lt y \lt 1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}_{Y}(y) & =P(Y\le y) \\  & =P(1-3X\le y) \\  & =P(-3X\le y-1) \\  & =P(X\ge \frac{1-y}{3}) \\  & =1-{F}_{X}\left(\frac{1-y}{3}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

To compute the PDF $f_Y(y)$ for $-2 \lt y \lt 1,$ we differentiate $F_Y$ with respect to $y$ using the chain rule. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={F}_{Y}^{′}(y) \\  & =0-\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)\cdot {F}_{X}^{′}\left(\frac{1-y}{3}\right) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot {f}_{X}\left(\frac{1-y}{3}\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the definition of $f_X,$ we finally arrive at

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot {f}_{X}\left(\frac{1-y}{3}\right) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot 2\cdot \left(\frac{1-y}{3}\right) \\  & =\frac{2}{9}(1-y).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the full expression for the PDF of $Y$ is

$$
f_Y(y) =  
	{\left\{  \begin{array}{ll}{\displaystyle \frac{2}{9}} ( 1 - y ) , \hspace{1em} & - 2 < y < 1 \\ 0 , \hspace{1em} & \text{otherwise}\end{array} \right. }
$$

$$
If $Y = (2-X)^3,$ then what is the probability density function of $Y?$

To compute the probability density function of a random variable $Y,$ where $Y = u(X)$ is a continuous, strictly monotonic function of a continuous random variable $X,$ we follow two steps:

- First, we find an expression for $F_Y$ terms of $F_X,$ where $F_Y$ and $F_X$ are the cumulative distribution functions of $Y$ and $X,$ respectively.

- Then, we differentiate $F_Y$ to get the probability density function $f_Y.$

Before we start, note that $Y = (2-X)^3$ is a strictly decreasing function of $X.$ Moreover, for $0 \lt x \lt 2,$ we have $0 \lt y \lt 8 .$

![](images/2c/2c07ffe5af282ba1689cb6f49201b979afb4186d0128dd6a97f446b7240d76d6.png)

 

Now, using the definition of the cumulative distribution of $Y,$ for $0 \lt y \lt 8,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}_{Y}(y) & =P(Y\le y) \\  & =P((2-X)^{3}\le y) \\  & =P(2-X\le {y}^{1/3}) \\  & =P(-X\le {y}^{1/3}-2) \\  & =P(X\ge 2-{y}^{1/3}) \\  & =1-{F}_{X}(2-{y}^{1/3}).\end{aligned}
$$

To compute the PDF $f_Y(y)$ for $0 \lt y \lt 8,$ we differentiate $F_Y$ with respect to $y$ using the chain rule. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={F}_{Y}^{′}(y) \\  & =0-\left(-\frac{1}{3{y}^{2/3}}\right)\cdot {F}_{X}^{′}(2-{y}^{1/3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3{y}^{2/3}}\cdot {f}_{X}(2-{y}^{1/3}).\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the definition of $f_X,$ we finally arrive at

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & =\frac{1}{3{y}^{2/3}}\cdot {f}_{X}(2-{y}^{1/3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3{y}^{2/3}}\cdot \frac{3}{8}(2-(2-{y}^{1/3}))^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3{y}^{2/3}}\cdot \frac{3}{8}(2-2+{y}^{1/3})^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3{y}^{2/3}}\cdot \frac{3}{8}({y}^{1/3})^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the full expression for the PDF of $Y$ is

$$
f_Y(y) =

- $\lambda=-1$ of algebraic multiplicity $2$

- $\lambda=3$ of algebraic multiplicity $1$

As a result, we have one $1 \times 1$ Jordan block $J_1(3)$ corresponding to $\lambda=3.$
However, there are two possibilities for the Jordan blocks corresponding to $\lambda=-1{:}$

- *Case I.* We may get the single $2 \times 2$ Jordan block $J_2(-1).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors $\mathbf v_1$ and $\mathbf v_2$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda=-1$ form the following chain:

$$
\mathbf{v}_2 \xrightarrow{A+I} \mathbf{v}_1 \xrightarrow{A+I} \mathbf{0}
$$

- *Case II.* We may get a composition of two $1 \times 1$ Jordan blocks, namely $J_1(-1) {\:\oplus\:} J_1(-1).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors $\mathbf v_1$ and $\mathbf v_2$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda=-1$ form the following chains:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\overset{A+I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {v}_{2}\overset{A+I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

To figure out which of the cases we obtain in this situation, let's find the number of linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda=-1.$

Computing $A+I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A+I & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 8 & 8 \\ 4 & 7 & 8 \\ -4 & -8 & -9\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 8 & 8 \\ 4 & 8 & 8 \\ -4 & -8 & -8\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce this matrix to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A+I & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 8 & 8 \\ 4 & 8 & 8 \\ -4 & -8 & -8\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}4 & 8 & 8 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -4 & -8 & -8\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}4 & 8 & 8 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\text{nullity}(A+I)=2,$ there will be two eigenvectors that correspond to the eigenvalue $\lambda=-1,$ say, $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2.$ So, the generalized eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda=-1$ form the following chains: 

$$
\mathbf{v}_1 \xrightarrow{A+I} \mathbf{0} \[5pt]
\mathbf{v}_2 \xrightarrow{A+I} \mathbf{0}
$$

Therefore, we have *case II*, and $A$ has the following Jordan canonical form:

$$
J_1(3) {\:\oplus\:} J_1(-1) {\:\oplus\:} J_1(-1) = 
{\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & - 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & - 1\end{array} \right]}
$$

**Note:** The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks.

First, let's remind ourselves of some basic facts.

- Given a random variable $X \sim U[\alpha, \beta]$, the probability density function (PDF) of $X$ is given by
$$
\displaystyle f(x) =
    {\left\{  \begin{array}{ll}{\displaystyle \frac{1}{\beta  - \alpha }} , \hspace{2em} & a \le  x \le  b , \\ 0 , & \text{otherwise.}\end{array} \right. }
$$
- For any interval $[x_1, x_2] \subseteq [\alpha, \beta]$, the probability that $X$ lies within that interval is
$$
\displaystyle P(x_1 \leq X \leq x_2) = \displaystyle \int_{x_1}^{x_2} f(x) \, dx = \dfrac{x_2 - x_1}{\beta-\alpha}.
$$
- If we divide the range $[\alpha, \beta]$ into $k$ intervals, then the expected frequency of observations falling in the $i$th interval $[x_{i-1}, x_i]$ is given by
$$
\displaystyle E_i = N \cdot P(x_{i-1} \leq X \leq x_i) = N \cdot \dfrac{x_i - x_{i-1}}{\beta-\alpha}.
$$

Let's once again consider the line integral with respect to arc length of $f(x,y)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\displaystyle\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s
$$

There are two more important properties of this type of line integral that we need to be aware of.

- There is usually more than one way to parametrize a curve. However, line integrals with respect to arc length are *independent of the choice of parametrization*. In other words, we get the same result regardless of which parametrization we choose.

For example, the paths $C_1$ and $C_2,$ given by 

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}_{1}:\,{r}_{1}(t) & =⟨\operatorname{cos}t,\,\operatorname{sin}t⟩, & 0\le t<2\pi  \\ {C}_{2}:\,{r}_{2}(u) & =⟨\operatorname{cos}2u,\,\operatorname{sin}2u⟩, & 0\le u<\pi \end{aligned}
$$

both traverse a circle of radius $1$ once in the counterclockwise direction starting from $(1,0).$ However, since line integrals with respect to arc length are independent of parametrization, we have

$$
\displaystyle\int\limits_{C_1} f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s = \displaystyle\int\limits_{C_2} f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s
$$

- Line integrals with respect to arc length are also *independent of the orientation* of $C.$ For example, suppose that $C$ is a path along a particular curve traversed from the point $A$ to the point $B.$ Then, $-C$ is a path along the same curve but traversed from $B$ to $A,$ as shown below.

![](images/e4/e4f68e10429fa4bda69366751c303216d27df995edf2502b61ab9bfe84c3ff45.png)

Independence of orientation means that

$$
\displaystyle\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s = \displaystyle\int\limits_{-C} f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s.
$$

- Finally, it's important to mention that all of the properties discussed in this lesson apply to line integrals with respect to arc length over space curves, i.e., line integrals of the form $$
\displaystyle\int_{C} f(x,y,z)\,\textrm d s.
$$

and its singular value decomposition $A=U \Sigma V ^T,$ where

$$
U = {\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}{\displaystyle \frac{4}{5}} & 0 & - {\displaystyle \frac{3}{5}} \\ {\displaystyle \frac{3}{5}} & 0 & {\displaystyle \frac{4}{5}} \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{array} \right]},

	\quad
	V = {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{array} \right]}.
$$

Notice that $\Sigma$ contains a row of zeros. In these situations, it's possible to simplify the decomposition of $A.$ This simplified decomposition is called the **reduced singular value decomposition** of $A.$

First, we note that $A$ is a $3 \times 2$ matrix. In addition, the matrix $\Sigma$ has two non-zero singular values on its main diagonal, so the rank of $A$ is $\color{blue}r=2.$ 

To find our reduced SVD, we proceed as follows:

- First, we remove all zero rows and columns from $\Sigma.$ In our example, we should delete the $3$rd row since it contains only zeros. Notice that we obtain a square invertible matrix of rank ${\color{blue}2}{:}$ 
$$
\Sigma={\left[ \begin{array}{cc}{\color{blue}5} & 0 \\ 0 & {\color{blue}2} \\ \hline {\color{red}0} & {\color{red}0}\end{array} \right]} \qquad \longrightarrow \qquad  \Sigma_r= {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{array} \right]}
$$

- Next, we remove all extra columns of $U$ starting from the right, keeping only $\color{blue}2$ columns. In our example, we should delete the $3$rd column:
$$
U=\left[{\begin{array}{cc|c}{\displaystyle \frac{4}{5}} & 0 & {\color{red}- {\displaystyle \frac{3}{5}}} \\ {\displaystyle \frac{3}{5}} & 0 & {\color{red}{\displaystyle \frac{4}{5}}} \\ 0 & 1 & {\color{red}0}\end{array}}\right]
\qquad \longrightarrow \qquad 
U_r={\left[ \begin{array}{cc}{\displaystyle \frac{4}{5}} & 0 \\ {\displaystyle \frac{3}{5}} & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{array} \right]}.
$$

- Finally, we remove all extra columns of $V$ starting from the right, keeping only $\color{blue}2$ columns. In our example, we should keep $V$ as it is since it already has only $2$ columns: 
$$
V={\left[ \begin{array}{cc}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{array} \right]}
\qquad \longrightarrow \qquad 
V_r={\left[ \begin{array}{cc}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{array} \right]}
$$

The reduced singular value decomposition of $A$ is then given by

$$
A = U_r \Sigma_r V_r^T.
$$

So, in our example, we have

$$
A= {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}{\displaystyle \frac{4}{5}} & 0 \\ {\displaystyle \frac{3}{5}} & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{array} \right]} 
{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{array} \right]}
{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{array} \right]}^T.

Suppose that $A$ is a $m\times n$ matrix, and 

$$
A=U \Sigma V^T
$$

is a singular value decomposition of $A.$ If the $i$th singular value of $A$ is nonzero, then the $i$th column of the orthogonal matrix $U$ can be found using the formula

$$
\mathbf{u}_i = \dfrac{1}{\sigma_i} A\mathbf{v}_i,
$$

 

where $\mathbf u_i$ and $\mathbf v_i$ are the $i$th columns of the orthogonal matrices $U$ and $V,$ respectively.  

The formula above works whenever $\sigma_i\neq 0.$ But how do we find the $i$th column of $U$ in cases where $\sigma_i = 0?$ It turns out that we can find the corresponding left singular vector using the geometric properties of singular values.

For example, suppose that

$$
A ={\left[ \begin{array}{cc}\sqrt{3} & 1 \\ 3 & \sqrt{3}\end{array} \right]},
$$

and $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ where
$$
\Sigma = {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{array} \right]}, 
	\qquad
	V = {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}{\displaystyle \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}} & - {\displaystyle \frac{1}{2}} \\ {\displaystyle \frac{1}{2}} & {\displaystyle \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}}\end{array} \right]}.
$$
The matrices $\Sigma$ and $V$ can be found using the methods we've seen before. So, our task now is to find the matrix $U.$ 

From $\Sigma,$ we deduce that the singular values of $A$ are $\sigma_1=4$ and $\sigma_2=0.$ Therefore, the first column of $U$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{3} & 1 \\ 3 & \sqrt{3}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ \frac{1}{2}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since the second singular value is $\sigma_2=0$, we can't use the same formula to find the second column of $U.$ However, we know that $U$ is an orthogonal matrix. Hence, we must find a vector

$$
\mathbf{u}_2 =  {\left[ \begin{array}{c}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{array} \right]}
$$

such that 

$$
\mathbf{u}_1 \cdot \mathbf{u}_2 = 0 \qquad \textrm{and} \qquad \|\mathbf{u}_2\|=1.
$$

 

Let's consider each condition in turn:

- The equation $\mathbf{u}_1 \cdot \mathbf{u}_2 = 0$  is equivalent to

$$
\dfrac{1}{{2}} x_1 +  \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} x_2 = 0.
$$

Seeking a nonzero solution to this equation, we get the vector 
$$
{\left[ \begin{array}{c}- \sqrt{3} \\ 1\end{array} \right]}.
$$

- Normalizing the vector we just found, we get
$$
\mathbf{u}_2 = \dfrac12{\left[ \begin{array}{c}- \sqrt{3} \\ 1\end{array} \right]} = {\left[ \begin{array}{c}- {\displaystyle \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}} \\ {\displaystyle \frac{1}{2}}\end{array} \right]}.
$$

Therefore, our orthogonal matrix $U$ is given by

$$
U= {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}{\displaystyle \frac{1}{2}} & - {\displaystyle \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}} \\ {\displaystyle \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}} & {\displaystyle \frac{1}{2}}\end{array} \right]}.
$$

One use for finding the orthogonal projection of a vector onto a subspace is to find the shortest distance between the vector and the subspace.

Given a vector $\mathbf{x}$ and a subspace $S = \textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \},$ the **distance between $\mathbf{x}$ and $S$** is given by 

$$
\Vert \mathbf{x} - \textrm{proj}_{S}\mathbf{x} \Vert
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/d1/d10fd1778529183deb6912cebe9d2b7ad405091fe21a261c464d3d22c6d0860b.png)

Let's find the distance between the vector $\mathbf{x}$ and the subspace spanned by the linearly independent vectors $\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2 \},$ where

$$
\mathbf{a}_1={\left[ \begin{array}{c}1 \\ 0 \\ - 1\end{array} \right]},\quad
	\mathbf{a}_2={\left[ \begin{array}{c}2 \\ - 1 \\ - 2\end{array} \right]},
	\qquad
	\mathbf{x}={\left[ \begin{array}{c}0 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{array} \right]}.
$$

The orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
\textrm{proj}_{S} \: \mathbf{x} = A(A^T\!A)^{-1}\!A^T\,\mathbf{x}.
$$

In this case, we have 
$$
A
={\left[ \begin{array}{cc}| & | \\ {\mathbf{a}}_{1} & {\mathbf{a}}_{2} \\ | & |\end{array} \right]} 
={\left[ \begin{array}{cc}1 & 2 \\ 0 & - 1 \\ - 1 & - 2\end{array} \right]} \qquad \Longrightarrow\qquad A^T={\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}1 & 0 & - 1 \\ 2 & - 1 & - 2\end{array} \right]}.
$$
Therefore, we get the following projection: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{bmatrix}\cdot {(\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & -1 \\ 2 & -1 & -2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{bmatrix})}^{-1}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & -1 \\ 2 & -1 & -2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{bmatrix}\cdot {\begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 \\ 4 & 9\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ -10\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}9 & -4 \\ -4 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ -10\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}=\hat{x}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, using the distance formula, the distance between $\mathbf{x}$ and the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}d(x,\hat{x}) & =‖x-\hat{x}‖ \\  & =\sqrt{({x}_{1}-{\hat{x}}_{1})^{2}+({x}_{2}-{\hat{x}}_{2})^{2}+({x}_{3}-{\hat{x}}_{3})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(0-(-2))^{2}+(2-2)^{2}+(4-2)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4+0+4} \\  & =\sqrt{8} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** Recall that the vector $\textbf{x}-\textrm{proj}_{S}\,\mathbf{x},$ whose norm $\| \textbf{x}-\textrm{proj}_{S}\,\mathbf{x} \|$ represents the distance from $\mathbf{x}$ to $S,$ is sometimes called the **vector rejection of $\mathbf{x}$ from $S.$**

As well as finding the distance between a vector and a subspace, we can also use the vector's orthogonal projection onto the subspace to find the angle between the vector and the subspace.

Given a vector $\mathbf{x}$ and a subspace $S = \textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \},$ the **acute angle between $\mathbf{x}$ and $S$** is the acute angle formed by $\mathbf{x}$ and its orthogonal projection $\textrm{proj}_S \mathbf{x},$ as shown below:

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x=-3$ and $y=5$, which can be written as $(-3,5)$.

Consider the following system of equations:

$$
{\left\{  \begin{array}{l}{\color{red}5} x + 2 y = - 1 \\ - {\color{blue}4} x - 3 y = - 2\end{array} \right. }
$$

Suppose we want to eliminate the variable $x$ from the system using the elimination method.

First, notice that the coefficient of $x$ in the *first* equation is ${\color{red}{5}}$, while in the *second* equation it is $-{\color{blue}{4}}$.

So, if we multiply the *first* equation by ${\color{blue}{4}}$ and the *second* equation by ${\color{red}{5}}$, then the $x$-coefficient in the first and second equations respectively will become $20$ and $-20$, and these will cancel when we add the equations.

$$
{\left\{  \begin{array}{l}( \hspace{0.167em} {\color{red}5} x + 2 y = - 1 \hspace{0.167em} ) \hspace{0.222em} \times  ( {\color{blue}4} ) \\ ( \hspace{0.167em} - {\color{blue}4} x - 3 y = - 2 \hspace{0.167em} ) \hspace{0.222em} \times  ( {\color{red}5} )\end{array} \right. }
	\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
	{\left\{  \begin{array}{l}20 x + 8 y = - 4 \\ - 20 x - 15 y = - 10\end{array} \right. }
$$

Now, when we add the two equations, the variable $x$ will be eliminated:

$$
{\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle \cancel{20 x} + 8 y & \displaystyle  = - 4 \\ \displaystyle - \cancel{20 x} - 15 y & \displaystyle  = - 10 \\ \hline \displaystyle ( 8 y - 15 y ) & \displaystyle  = ( - 4 - 10 ) \\ \displaystyle - 7 y & \displaystyle  = - 14 \\ \displaystyle y & \displaystyle  = 2\end{array}}
$$

Therefore, we have successfully eliminated the variable $x$ from the system.

Now that we've learned how to calculate the mean of a data set from a frequency table, let's consider how we'd calculate a missing frequency given the mean of a data set.

Consider the frequency table below, where the frequency associated with the value $x=9$ is unknown.

| Value $(x)$ | Frequency $(f_x)$ |
| --- | ---: |
| $2$ | $2$ |
| $6$ | $2$ |
| $9$ | $$? |
| $13$ | $9$ |

Suppose we're given that the mean of the dataset is $10$. How can we use this to find the missing frequency?

To find the missing frequency, let's first extend the table to include a third column for the product of each value and its frequency, as before.

| Value ($x$) | Frequency ($f_x$) | $x \cdot f_x$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| $2$ | $\color{blue}2$ | $2 \cdot 2 = {\color{red}{4}}\:\:\quad$ |
| $6$ | $\color{blue}2$ | $6 \cdot 2 = {\color{red}{12}}\quad$ |
| $9$ | $\color{blue}f_{9}$ | ${\color{red}{9\cdot f_9}}\:\:\qquad$ |
| $13$ | $\color{blue}9$ | $13 \cdot 9 = {\color{red}{117}}\:\:$ |

Notice that we've denoted the missing frequency as $f_9$.

Now, we find an expression for the mean by dividing the sum of these products by the total number of data points:

$$
\begin{aligned}
Mean &= \frac{4 + 12 + 9f_{9} + 117}{2 + 2 + f_{9} + 9} \\
&= \frac{133 + 9f_{9}}{13 + f_{9}}
\end{aligned}
$$

We are told that the mean of the dataset is $10$. So, we must have

$$
\dfrac{133 + 9f_{9}}{13 + f_{9}} = 10
$$

To compute the missing frequency, we must solve this rational equation.

First, we eliminate the denominator by multiplying both sides by $(13 + f_{9})$ before solving for $f_{9}{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
133 + 9f_{9} &= 10(13 + f_{9}) \\
133 + 9f_{9} &= 130 + 10f_{9} \\
9f_{9} - 10f_{9} &= 130 - 133 \\
- f_{9} &= -3 \\
f_{9} &= 3
\end{aligned}
$$

Now that we know the missing frequency, we can complete the table.

| Value | Frequency |
| --- | ---: |
| $2$ | $2$ |
| $6$ | $2$ |
| $9$ | $3$ |
| $13$ | $9$ |

In this lesson, we'll explore some techniques for solving systems of equations efficiently.

To motivate our discussion, let's consider the system of equations below.

$$
{\left\{  \begin{array}{l}7 x + 10 y = 80 \\ 10 x + 7 y = 73\end{array} \right. }
$$

Suppose we want to determine the quantity $x+y$. What's the easiest way to do this?

When solving systems of linear equations, two primary techniques are available: the substitution method and the elimination method.

- To solve this using *substitution*, we might start by expressing the first equation in terms of the variable $y$. By doing this, we get
$y =-\dfrac{7}{10}x + 10$.
Notice we've introduced a fraction, which makes the remaining steps more awkward.
- To solve this using *elimination*, on the other hand, we might choose to multiply the first equation by $7$ (the coefficient of $y$ in the second equation), the second equation by $10$ (the coefficient of $y$ in the first equation), before subtracting them to eliminate $y{:}$
$$
{\left\{  \begin{array}{l}( \hspace{0.167em} 7 x + {\color{red}10} y = 80 \hspace{0.167em} ) \hspace{0.222em} \times  ( {\color{blue}7} ) \\ ( \hspace{0.167em} 10 x + {\color{blue}7} y = 73 \hspace{0.167em} ) \hspace{0.222em} \times  ( {\color{red}10} )\end{array} \right. }
	\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
	{\left\{  \begin{array}{l}49 x + 70 y = 560 \\ 100 x + 70 y = 730\end{array} \right. }
$$
The issue now is that we've created a system containing very large numbers.

It turns out that we can exploit the system's symmetry to solve it more efficiently. We'll talk about this next.
